deep.reconstruction:
Context: the page is part of Riemann's Nachlass paper 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsaetze ueber lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten' (dated Goettingen, 20 Febr. 1857 on the next page). A 'system' (y_1,...,y_n) is an n-tuple of functions of x that are many-valued only at branch values a,b,...,g (p branch points in total, counting x later), and that undergo linear substitutions (A),(B),... around them. The notation \mathfrak{A}^{-1}(y) denotes the system transformed into the canonical branches at a, each of the form (x-a)^{alpha_i} times a power series in (x-a). The 'exponents' are the lowest powers occurring there, and the 'Exponentensumme' is the sum of all of them over all branch points.

The previous page found the most general system Y with the same substitutions and the same exponents as y. It has the form Y = k y + k_1 Y^(1) + ... + k_m Y^(m) with arbitrary constants k, k_1, ..., k_m.

Step 1 (this page). Fix the constants one at a time as functions of the remaining ones. Each time, choose them so that the leading coefficient (Anfangsglied) in the expansion of one of \mathfrak{A}^{-1}(Y), ..., \mathfrak{G}^{-1}(Y) vanishes. Each such condition raises one exponent by at least 1. After m steps the exponent sum has risen by at least m, and the number of free constants has dropped by m. Implicit step (mine): the process terminates because, for fixed substitutions, the exponent sum is bounded above (a Fuchs-type relation, used on earlier pages).

Step 2. The result is the 'reduced' system: maximal exponents within its class. It is determined by its characteristic (substitutions plus exponents) up to a common constant factor. Normalize by setting to 1 the coefficient of the lowest power of (x-a) in the first component of \mathfrak{A}^{-1}(y). The functions y are then uniquely determined by the data (a,...,g; (A),...,(F); exponents).

Step 3. Riemann now regards a branch point, say a, as variable and keeps the substitutions constant. Analytic continuation of this uniquely normalized object in a gives the theorem: the y_i, as functions of a, again form a system of the same kind. Its branch values are b,c,...,g,x, and its substitutions are composed of (A),...,(F). In modern terms, an isomonodromic deformation exists, and the normalized solution is a multivalued function of all p variables a,...,g,x. Its monodromy in the parameters lies in the group generated by the given matrices; this is spelled out on the next page.

Step 4 (degenerate case). It may be impossible to vary a with all substitutions held constant, because the free constants are fewer than the conditions. In that case one views the system as a special case of a system with lower exponents. For those special values of a,...,g, the leading coefficients of some initial terms in \mathfrak{A}^{-1}(y), ... vanish. This is an early version of the observation that the normalized isomonodromic family degenerates (jumps) on an exceptional set of parameter values. Compare the Malgrange divisor and the movable poles behind the Painleve property.

Marginal note in faint pencil ('das hier ist nicht richtig'?), hand uncertain: possibly Riemann's or an editor's (Weber's/Dedekind's) doubt about the counting argument or the degenerate-case claim.
errors: Possible slip in the text as transcribed: the exponent sum is first said to be 'erniedrigt' (lowered) by at least one each step, then 'erhoeht' (raised) by at least m overall. Making leading coefficients vanish raises exponents, so 'erhoeht' is correct. Either the manuscript has a slip or the transcription misreads the word.

Unjustified step: the claim that the free constants and the vanishing conditions can always be matched one-to-one is asserted without proof. It may fail if several conditions become dependent, which is precisely the degenerate case handled at the end only heuristically.

The central theorem (existence of a deformation in a with constant substitutions) is sketched only: 'man hat nur noethig scharf aufzufassen'. No argument is given for analyticity in a, nor that the varied object stays a system of the same type. Modern treatments (Schlesinger 1905; Malgrange 1983; Miwa 1981) need more work, in particular around the exceptional set where the normalization breaks down. The faint marginal remark 'nicht richtig' may refer to this.
Statement that the substitutions in the a-variable are 'composed of (A),...,(F)' is correct in spirit (the braid/pure-braid action on monodromy) but is stated vaguely.

results.what: Reduction of a system with prescribed monodromy and exponents to one with maximal exponent sum, unique up to a constant factor, by killing leading coefficients
results.modern_name: Normalization / maximal (reduced) solution in a monodromy class; precursor of Riemann–Hilbert normalization (Birkhoff/Plemelj normal forms, Levelt-type filtrations)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857 Nachlass, published in Werke 1876); later Plemelj, Birkhoff

results.what: Theorem: the normalized functions y, as functions of a branch point a, form a system of the same type with branch points b,...,g,x and substitutions composed of the given ones
results.modern_name: Isomonodromic deformation; Schlesinger system; multivalued dependence on the poles (pure braid group action on monodromy)
results.usually_credited_to: L. Schlesinger (1905), R. Fuchs (1905/1907); Riemann's 1857 statement is recognized as the germ

results.what: Degenerate parameter values where the normalized system cannot be continued with fixed exponents and appears as a special case of a lower-exponent system (vanishing leading coefficients)
results.modern_name: Exceptional set / Malgrange theta-divisor of isomonodromic deformations (movable poles, Painleve property)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the published (Werke) 1857 paper 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsaetze'. Riemann's anticipation of isomonodromic deformation is well known to historians. The degenerate-case remark is a nice detail but is in the published text, so it is not new.

checkable.sympy: x,a,b,al,be=symbols('x a b alpha beta'); y=(x-a)**al*(x-b)**be; simplify(diff(y,a) - (-al/(x-a))*y)==0
checkable.asserts: In the rank-1 model, varying a branch point a gives d y/da = -alpha/(x-a) y. This is a Fuchsian equation in a, singular at a=x with exponent alpha, illustrating that y is a 'system' in a with branch point x.
Translation invariance: dy/dx + dy/da = 0, so the dependence on a mirrors the dependence on x (the 'similar system in a').

Fuchs relation for an n-th order Fuchsian equation with p singular points (including infinity): the sum of exponents is (p-2)n(n-1)/2. For n=2, p=3 this gives 1, the Riemann P-symbol condition. This bounds the exponent sum and justifies termination of the raising procedure.

checkable.sympy: x,a,b,c,A,B,C=symbols('x a b c A B C'); expr=A/(x-a)+B/(x-b)+C/(x-c); simplify(diff(expr,a)-A/(x-a)**2)==0
checkable.asserts: Building block of the Schlesinger equations: d/da [A/(x-a)] = A/(x-a)^2 for constant residue A. Used when verifying that a Fuchsian system with a-dependent residues dA/da = [A,B]/(a-b) + ... is isomonodromic.

Right margin: page number '20' and a faint pencil note, read roughly as 'das hier ist nicht richtig'; the reading and the hand are uncertain.
'\mathfrak{G}^{-1}(y)' in line 2: the last letter of the series of fraktur symbols is uncertain (could be \mathfrak{G} or \mathfrak{F}); the substitutions are listed as (A),...,(F) later.
